topics.name: Subduction
topics.kicker: One plate diving beneath another into the mantle · Builds trenches and volcanoes
topics.dates: Ongoing all around the Pacific Ring of Fire
topics.briefing: Subduction happens where two tectonic plates collide and the denser one, usually made of old, cold ocean floor, bends and slides down beneath the other into the mantle. The sinking plate carves a deep trench, like the Mariana Trench, and water squeezed out of it helps melt the rock above, feeding chains of volcanoes. Subduction zones ring the Pacific Ocean and cause the world’s largest earthquakes.
topics.answerHtml: Subduction (accept subduction zones or subducting plates; prompt on convergent boundaries or Benioff zones; do not accept “seafloor spreading,” “obduction,” or “trenches”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Japanese seismologist Kiyoo Wadati and American Hugo Benioff mapped the tilted zones of earthquakes that follow this process downward into the mantle. The deepest of those earthquakes strike about 700 kilometers down, deeper than earthquakes reach anywhere else.
tossups.r: This process carves deep ocean trenches along the edges of the Pacific. For 10 points, name this process in which one tectonic plate sinks beneath another.

tossups.p: Water squeezed out of a sinking slab lowers the melting point of the hot mantle rock above it, a process called flux melting that feeds the volcanoes above zones of this process. Many of those volcanoes erupt andesite, a rock named for a South American mountain range.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process that builds the volcanoes of the Pacific Ring of Fire as one plate dives beneath another.

tossups.p: Mud and sand scraped off the top of a descending plate pile up into an accretionary wedge, or prism, at the edge of the overriding plate during this process. The island of Barbados sits on top of one of these scraped-up piles.
tossups.r: Where the descending plate bends downward, it forms a deep trench in the ocean floor. For 10 points, name this process in which one plate slides beneath another at a convergent boundary.

tossups.p: In 1960, Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh rode the bathyscaphe _Trieste_ down to the Challenger Deep, and in 2012 James Cameron made a solo dive to the same spot. That spot lies where the Pacific plate sinks beneath a smaller plate in this process.
tossups.r: That spot is in the Mariana Trench, the deepest part of the ocean. For 10 points, name this process in which one plate dives beneath another.

tossups.p: The strongest earthquake ever recorded, a magnitude 9.5 quake near Valdivia, Chile, in 1960, struck where the Nazca plate dives beneath South America in this process. Such “megathrust” earthquakes are the largest kind on Earth.
tossups.r: This process also raised the Andes Mountains. For 10 points, name this process in which an oceanic plate sinks beneath another plate into the mantle.

tossups.p: Many geologists think “slab pull,” the tug of a cold, dense plate sinking into the mantle during this process, is the strongest force moving tectonic plates. Because this process destroys old ocean floor, almost none of the seafloor is older than about 200 million years.
tossups.r: This process happens at convergent boundaries. For 10 points, name this process in which one plate dives beneath another at a deep ocean trench.

tossups.p: Most of the ancient Farallon [“FAIR-uh-lon”] plate has disappeared beneath western North America through this process, and the Juan de Fuca and Cocos plates are among its last surviving pieces. The Juan de Fuca plate still sinks beneath the Pacific Northwest, feeding volcanoes like Mount Rainier.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process in which a dense oceanic plate dives beneath another plate into the mantle.

tossups.p: Blueschist, a metamorphic rock colored blue by the mineral glaucophane [“GLAW-kuh-fayn”], forms under high pressure but fairly low temperature as rock is dragged deep during this process. Blueschist in California’s Coast Ranges marks where this process happened long ago.
tossups.r: This process occurs all around the Pacific Ring of Fire. For 10 points, name this process in which one tectonic plate slides beneath another.

tossups.p: The 2011 Tohoku [“TOH-hoh-koo”] earthquake and tsunami, which damaged the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear plant, struck where the Pacific plate sinks beneath northern Japan in this process. Japan itself is an island arc, a curving chain of volcanic islands built by this process.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process at convergent boundaries in which one tectonic plate dives beneath another.

tossups.p: Japanese records of a mysterious tsunami that arrived in January 1700 without any felt earthquake helped scientists date a giant quake along the Cascadia zone of this process, off the coast of the Pacific Northwest.
tossups.r: There, the Juan de Fuca plate sinks beneath North America. For 10 points, name this process in which one plate dives beneath another into the mantle.

tossups.p: In 1964, the strongest earthquake in U.S. history, a magnitude 9.2 quake centered on Alaska’s Prince William Sound, struck along a zone of this process. Farther west, the same zone has built the Aleutian Islands, a curving island arc.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process in which a dense oceanic plate sinks beneath another plate at a deep trench.

tossups.p: Harry Hess reasoned that if new ocean floor is always forming at mid-ocean ridges, old ocean floor must be destroyed somewhere else by this process, or else Earth would have to keep growing larger. Hess called his 1962 paper on the idea “an essay in geopoetry.”
tossups.r: This process happens where old seafloor sinks at deep ocean trenches. For 10 points, name this process in which one plate dives beneath another into the mantle.

tossups.p: This process’s name comes from Latin roots meaning “under” and “to lead.” In a related but much rarer process called obduction, slices of ocean crust are shoved up onto the edge of a continent instead of sinking.
tossups.r: This process makes deep trenches like the Mariana Trench. For 10 points, name this process in which one plate sinks beneath another into the mantle.

tossups.p: The 2004 Indian Ocean earthquake, whose tsunami struck coasts from Indonesia to East Africa, began off the island of Sumatra, along the Sunda megathrust created by this process. The same process built Indonesia’s many volcanoes, including Krakatoa.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process at convergent boundaries in which one tectonic plate dives beneath another into the mantle.

tossups.p: The Andes and the Cascades are volcanic mountain chains built by this process, and water released during it lowers the melting point of rock in the mantle. It recycles old, cold seafloor back into Earth’s interior.
tossups.r: In this process, a dense oceanic plate dives beneath a lighter plate at a convergent boundary. For 10 points, name this process that forms deep ocean trenches like the Mariana Trench.

clues.t: One tectonic plate sinks beneath another and descends into the mantle
The denser plate, usually old oceanic crust, goes down; lighter continental crust stays on top
Happens at convergent boundaries, where plates move toward each other
Carves deep ocean trenches, like the Mariana Trench, the deepest spot in the ocean
Builds most of the volcanoes and causes most of the earthquakes around the Pacific Ring of Fire
Builds curving island arcs (Japan, the Aleutians) or volcanic mountain chains on continents (the Andes, the Cascades)
Water squeezed from the sinking plate lowers the melting point of mantle rock above it: flux melting
Its volcanoes often erupt andesite, a rock named for the Andes
Causes the largest “megathrust” earthquakes, like the magnitude 9.5 Chile quake of 1960
The Nazca plate dives beneath South America, raising the Andes
The Juan de Fuca plate sinks beneath the Pacific Northwest, feeding Cascade volcanoes like Mount Rainier and Mount St. Helens
Destroys old ocean floor, so almost no seafloor is older than about 200 million years
“Slab pull,” the tug of the sinking plate, is thought to be the strongest force moving plates
Kiyoo Wadati and Hugo Benioff mapped the slanting zones of earthquakes along the sinking plate
Its deepest earthquakes strike about 700 km down, deeper than anywhere else
Sediment scraped off the sinking plate piles up in an accretionary wedge; Barbados sits on one
Piccard and Walsh reached the Challenger Deep in the _Trieste_ (1960); James Cameron dove there alone in 2012
Most of the ancient Farallon plate vanished beneath North America; the Juan de Fuca and Cocos plates are leftovers
Blueschist, colored blue by glaucophane, forms at high pressure but low temperature in its zones
The 2011 Tohoku earthquake and tsunami struck where the Pacific plate sinks beneath Japan
A Cascadia quake in January 1700 sent a tsunami to Japan that arrived with no felt earthquake
The magnitude 9.2 Alaska earthquake of 1964, the strongest in U.S. history, struck in one of its zones
The 2004 Indian Ocean earthquake and tsunami began off Sumatra; the same process built Krakatoa
Harry Hess said old seafloor must be destroyed at trenches, or Earth would keep growing
Name from Latin roots for “under” and “to lead”; in rarer obduction, ocean crust is pushed up onto land

trap.title: Process, not the trench
trap.body: Subduction tossups name its results, like the Mariana Trench, the Ring of Fire, island arcs, and giant earthquakes, so players blurt out one of those, which is wrong. Others answer “convergent boundary,” the kind of boundary where it happens, which earns only a prompt, or “seafloor spreading,” which makes new ocean floor instead of destroying it.
trap.fix: Listen for “this process” plus a plate sinking, diving, or descending beneath another: say subduction. If you are prompted after “convergent boundary,” add “subduction zone.” New crust forming at a ridge means seafloor spreading, and the whole theory of moving plates means plate tectonics.
trap.line: Real answer line: Subduction (accept subduction zones; prompt on convergent boundaries; do not accept “seafloor spreading” or “obduction”)

topics.name: Cambrian period
topics.kicker: First period of the Paleozoic Era · When most animal groups first appear
topics.briefing: The Cambrian period began about 539 million years ago, and over the next few tens of millions of years most major groups of animals appeared in the fossil record, a burst known as the Cambrian explosion. Trilobites crawled across the seafloor, while strange creatures like five-eyed Opabinia and the predator Anomalocaris swam above them. Canada’s Burgess Shale preserved many of these animals in amazing detail, even their soft parts.
topics.answerHtml: Cambrian period (accept Cambrian explosion; prompt on Paleozoic Era; do not accept “Precambrian” or “Ordovician”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In 1879, Charles Lapworth ended a long fight between Adam Sedgwick and Roderick Murchison by creating the Ordovician, made from rock layers that both men had claimed, and the Ordovician became the period right after this one.
tossups.r: Sedgwick named this period for an old Latin name for Wales. For 10 points, name this first period of the Paleozoic Era, known for an “explosion” of animal life.

tossups.p: In 1909, Charles Walcott, the head of the Smithsonian Institution, discovered a fossil bed high in the Canadian Rockies that preserves soft-bodied animals from this period in amazing detail. Walcott later described the early chordate Pikaia from those rocks.
tossups.r: That fossil bed is the Burgess Shale. For 10 points, name this period that began about 539 million years ago with an “explosion” of animal life.

tossups.p: When Simon Conway Morris named Hallucigenia [“huh-loo-sih-JEE-nee-uh”] from fossils of this period, he drew it upside down, mistaking its long spines for legs. He chose its name because the animal looked so strange and dreamlike.
tossups.r: It is one of many odd animals from the Burgess Shale. For 10 points, name this period known for a sudden burst, or “explosion,” of animal life.

tossups.p: The grasping front limbs of Anomalocaris [“uh-nom-uh-loh-KAIR-iss”], whose name means “abnormal shrimp,” were first mistaken for the tail ends of shrimp-like animals. This top predator, one of the largest animals of its time, hunted in the seas of this period.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this first period of the Paleozoic Era, when trilobites and many other animal groups first appeared.

tossups.p: Opabinia [“oh-puh-BIN-ee-uh”], an animal with five eyes on stalks and a long, flexible nozzle tipped with a grasping claw, swam in the seas of this period. Its fossils come from a famous shale in British Columbia’s Yoho National Park.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this period, known for the sudden appearance of most major animal groups in an event called its “explosion.”

tossups.p: Stephen Jay Gould’s book _Wonderful Life_ argued that the strange animals of this period show how much evolution depends on chance, but Simon Conway Morris, who studied many of the same fossils, disagreed. Gould published that book in 1989.
tossups.r: Those fossils come from the Burgess Shale. For 10 points, name this first period of the Paleozoic Era, famous for an “explosion” of animal diversity.

tossups.p: China’s Chengjiang [“chung-jyahng”] fossils, found in Yunnan Province, preserve soft-bodied animals from early in this period, including the fishlike Haikouichthys [“hy-koo-IK-thiss”], one of the earliest known chordates. Those fossils are about 10 million years older than Canada’s Burgess Shale.
tossups.r: Trilobites were common in this period. For 10 points, name this period, which began about 539 million years ago with an “explosion” of animal life.

tossups.p: Charles Darwin admitted in _On the Origin of Species_ that he could not explain why so many kinds of animals seemed to appear suddenly in the oldest fossil-rich rocks then known, which belong to this period, with almost no fossils of their ancestors beneath them.
tossups.r: Scientists call that burst of life this period’s “explosion.” For 10 points, name this period that came right before the Ordovician.

tossups.p: The start of this period is officially marked at Fortune Head in Newfoundland by the first appearance of Treptichnus pedum, a trace fossil left by a burrowing animal. Before this period, during the Ediacaran, soft, quilted creatures like Dickinsonia lay on the seafloor.
tossups.r: This period was followed by the Ordovician. For 10 points, name this first period of the Paleozoic Era.

tossups.p: In the Grand Canyon, the Tapeats Sandstone, Bright Angel Shale, and Muav Limestone formed during this period. They rest on far older rock across a gap in the rock record that John Wesley Powell named the Great Unconformity.
tossups.r: Trilobite fossils turn up in those layers. For 10 points, name this period, famous for its “explosion” of animal life.

tossups.p: Tiny tubes, cones, and plates of shell from early in this period are called “small shelly fossils,” and they show that many animals were starting to build hard parts. Hard shells and exoskeletons may have helped animals of this period protect themselves from new predators.
tossups.r: Trilobites, arthropods with three-lobed bodies, are this period’s most famous fossils. For 10 points, name this period, which began about 539 million years ago.

tossups.p: Sponge-like animals called archaeocyathids [“ar-kee-oh-SY-uh-thids”] built some of the first animal reefs early in this period, but nearly all of them vanished partway through it. During this period, life was still almost entirely in the sea, since plants had not yet spread onto land.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this first period of the Paleozoic Era, known for its sudden “explosion” of animal life.

tossups.p: Andrew Parker’s “Light Switch” hypothesis argues that the evolution of eyes set off an arms race between predators and prey during this period. Other scientists point to rising oxygen levels in the oceans as a trigger for this period’s changes.
tossups.r: Those changes produced most major animal groups in a burst called this period’s “explosion.” For 10 points, name this first period of the Paleozoic Era.

tossups.p: Marrella, a small arthropod with long, sweeping spines on its head shield, is the most common animal found in a famous fossil bed from this period. Underwater mudflows buried those animals so quickly that even their soft parts were preserved.
tossups.r: That fossil bed is Canada’s Burgess Shale. For 10 points, name this period that began about 539 million years ago, famous for its “explosion” of animal life.

tossups.p: Most major groups of animals first appear in the fossil record during this period, when trilobites crawled across the seafloor and the predator Anomalocaris hunted above them. Five-eyed Opabinia also lived in its seas.
tossups.r: This period came right before the Ordovician and saw a sudden burst of new animals called an “explosion.” For 10 points, name this first period of the Paleozoic Era.

clues.t: The first period of the Paleozoic Era
Known for its “explosion”: most major animal groups appear suddenly in the fossil record
Began about 539 million years ago, after billions of years of mostly single-celled life
Followed by the Ordovician period
Trilobites, three-lobed arthropods, are its most famous fossils
Canada’s Burgess Shale, in British Columbia’s Yoho National Park, preserves its soft-bodied animals in amazing detail
Charles Walcott, head of the Smithsonian, discovered the Burgess Shale in 1909 and described Pikaia
Adam Sedgwick named it in 1835 for the old Latin name for Wales
Anomalocaris (“abnormal shrimp”) was a top predator; its front limbs were first mistaken for shrimp-like animals
Opabinia had five eyes on stalks and a long nozzle tipped with a claw
Many animals first grew hard shells and exoskeletons; tiny early pieces are “small shelly fossils”
Charles Lapworth created the Ordovician in 1879 to settle the Sedgwick–Murchison fight over its rocks
Simon Conway Morris named Hallucigenia for its dreamlike look and first drew it upside down
Stephen Jay Gould’s _Wonderful Life_ (1989) used its fossils to argue that evolution depends on chance
China’s Chengjiang fossils, about 10 million years older than the Burgess Shale, include the fishlike Haikouichthys
Darwin admitted in _On the Origin of Species_ that he could not explain animals appearing so suddenly in its rocks
Its start is defined at Fortune Head, Newfoundland, by the burrow fossil Treptichnus pedum
It followed the Ediacaran period, home to soft, quilted creatures like Dickinsonia
The Grand Canyon’s Tapeats Sandstone, Bright Angel Shale, and Muav Limestone date from it, above Powell’s Great Unconformity
Marrella, a spiny little arthropod, is the most common Burgess Shale animal; mudflows buried the animals quickly
Sponge-like archaeocyathids built some of the first animal reefs; life was still almost all in the sea
Andrew Parker’s “Light Switch” idea: the evolution of eyes sparked a predator–prey arms race; rising oxygen is another proposed trigger

trap.title: Precambrian or Cambrian?
trap.body: The Precambrian is everything before this period, from Earth’s formation up to about 539 million years ago, so “Precambrian” is a different answer even though it contains this period’s name. The Ordovician came right after, and saying only “Paleozoic” names the whole era, which earns a prompt at most.
trap.fix: The Burgess Shale, early trilobites, Anomalocaris, Hallucigenia, and a sudden “explosion” of animals mean the Cambrian. Ediacaran creatures like Dickinsonia and the earliest single-celled life mean the Precambrian, and Charles Lapworth’s compromise period, with its later wave of new species, means the Ordovician.
trap.line: Real answer line: Cambrian period (accept Cambrian explosion; prompt on Paleozoic; do not accept “Precambrian” or “Ordovician”)

topics.name: El Niño
topics.kicker: Warming of the tropical Pacific every few years · Shifts weather worldwide
topics.briefing: Every few years, the trade winds over the tropical Pacific weaken, and a huge pool of warm water spreads east toward South America: that is El Niño. Peruvian fishermen named it “the boy,” meaning the Christ child, because the warm water often arrived around Christmas. It can wreck fish catches, flood deserts, and bring drought to Australia and Indonesia, and its cold opposite is called La Niña.
topics.answerHtml: El Niño (accept El Nino, El Niño–Southern Oscillation, or ENSO; prompt on Southern Oscillation; do not accept “La Niña”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: While trying to predict failures of India’s monsoon in the 1920s, Gilbert Walker discovered a seesaw in air pressure across the tropical Pacific and Indian Oceans, which he named the Southern Oscillation. That seesaw was later linked to this ocean event.
tossups.r: During this event, weak trade winds let warm water spread east toward South America. For 10 points, name this climate pattern, the opposite of La Niña.

tossups.p: Scientists often track this event with an index based on the difference in air pressure between Tahiti and Darwin, Australia, and that index turns negative while this event is under way. That index is called the Southern Oscillation Index.
tossups.r: Peruvian fishermen named this event for the Christ child because it often arrives near Christmas. For 10 points, name this warming of the eastern tropical Pacific.

tossups.p: Slow, eastward-moving bulges of warm water called Kelvin waves carry heat across the equatorial Pacific at the start of this event, pushing the thermocline deeper off South America. Bursts of westerly wind over the western Pacific can set those waves in motion.
tossups.r: This event weakens upwelling off Peru. For 10 points, name this warm phase of the tropical Pacific, the opposite of La Niña.

tossups.p: Galápagos marine iguanas can actually shrink in body length during this event, because the algae they graze on underwater die back. Galápagos penguins and sea lions also go hungry when this event cuts off their cold, food-rich water.
tossups.r: This event also hurts the anchoveta catch off Peru. For 10 points, name this periodic warming of the eastern Pacific Ocean, named for the Christ child.

tossups.p: The 1997–98 example of this event, one of the strongest ever measured, brought deadly floods to Peru and Ecuador and a stormy winter to California. It helped make 1998 the warmest year on record up to that time.
tossups.r: Its name means “the boy” in Spanish. For 10 points, name this warming of the tropical Pacific Ocean, the opposite of La Niña.

tossups.p: In 1972, Peru’s anchoveta fishery, then the largest in the world, collapsed when this event cut off the upwelling of nutrient-rich water, on top of years of heavy fishing. Seabirds that fed on those fish died in huge numbers.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this warming of the Pacific off South America, which Peruvian fishermen named for the Christ child.

tossups.p: This event usually weakens the Atlantic hurricane season, because it strengthens the high-altitude winds that shear the tops off growing storms, while the eastern Pacific often sees more strong storms. Forecasters call that effect wind shear.
tossups.r: It tends to bring wetter winters to the southern United States. For 10 points, name this periodic warming of the eastern tropical Pacific, whose cold counterpart is La Niña.

tossups.p: During this event, heavy rain shifts away from Indonesia and eastern Australia, bringing drought and wildfires there, while normally dry coastal deserts in Peru can flood. India’s summer monsoon also tends to be weaker.
tossups.r: This event happens when the trade winds weaken over the tropical Pacific. For 10 points, name this climate pattern that returns every two to seven years.

tossups.p: Scientists at NOAA declare this event when sea-surface temperatures in a key patch of the central Pacific stay at least 0.5 degrees Celsius above normal for several months in a row, along with matching changes in the winds above.
tossups.r: Its Spanish name refers to the Christ child. For 10 points, name this warm event in the tropical Pacific, the opposite of La Niña.

tossups.p: A version of this event centered in the middle of the Pacific, rather than near South America, has been nicknamed Modoki, from a Japanese word meaning “similar but different.” In that version, the water off South America can stay cooler than normal.
tossups.r: In the usual version, weak trade winds let warm water pile up off Peru. For 10 points, name this climate event whose cold opposite is La Niña.

tossups.p: After scientists failed to see the giant 1982–83 example of this event coming until it was well under way, they built the TAO array, a network of moored buoys across the equatorial Pacific that watches for it.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this periodic warming of the tropical Pacific that Peruvian fishermen named for the infant Jesus.

tossups.p: Jacob Bjerknes [“BYERK-ness”] explained this event in 1969 with a feedback loop between the ocean and the winds above it, in which a small warming in the eastern Pacific keeps growing stronger. He named the usual east–west loop of air over the Pacific the Walker circulation, after Gilbert Walker.
tossups.r: The Southern Oscillation is the air-pressure part of the same cycle. For 10 points, name this warm event in the Pacific, whose cold counterpart is La Niña.

tossups.p: The 2015–16 example of this event, one of the strongest on record, helped make 2016 the hottest year measured up to that time, and it helped cause severe coral bleaching on Australia’s Great Barrier Reef.
tossups.r: During this event, the trade winds weaken and warm water spreads east. For 10 points, name this climate pattern named for the Christ child.

tossups.p: During this event, the Pacific jet stream often shifts south and strengthens, steering storms toward California and the Gulf Coast while the northern United States and Canada have milder winters than usual.
tossups.r: This event weakens the upwelling of cold water off Peru. For 10 points, name this warming of the tropical Pacific, whose opposite is La Niña.

tossups.p: This event is one phase of a cycle that includes the Southern Oscillation, and it usually brings drought to Indonesia and Australia and fewer hurricanes to the Atlantic. It also shuts down the upwelling of cold water off Peru.
tossups.r: Peruvian fishermen named it for the Christ child because it often arrives near Christmas. For 10 points, name this warming of the eastern Pacific, the opposite of La Niña.

clues.t: A warming of the surface waters of the central and eastern tropical Pacific Ocean
Named by Peruvian fishermen for the Christ child, since it often arrives near Christmas; Spanish for “the boy”
Its cold opposite is La Niña (“the girl”)
Happens when the trade winds weaken and warm water spreads east toward South America
Returns every 2 to 7 years
Linked to the Southern Oscillation, a seesaw in air pressure across the tropical Pacific; together they form one cycle
Weakens the upwelling of cold, nutrient-rich water off Peru, hurting the anchoveta fishery
Brings drought and wildfires to Indonesia and eastern Australia, weakens India’s monsoon, and floods Peru’s coastal deserts
Usually weakens the Atlantic hurricane season by strengthening wind shear
The 1997–98 event, one of the strongest ever measured, flooded Peru and Ecuador and helped make 1998 the warmest year on record up to then
Often brings wetter winters to the southern U.S. and milder winters to the northern U.S. and Canada
The thermocline deepens in the eastern Pacific, so less cold water reaches the surface
Gilbert Walker found the Southern Oscillation in the 1920s while trying to predict India’s monsoon failures
Jacob Bjerknes explained it in 1969 with an ocean–wind feedback loop and named the Walker circulation
The Southern Oscillation Index compares air pressure at Tahiti and Darwin, Australia; it turns negative during the warm event
Eastward-moving Kelvin waves, set off by bursts of westerly wind, carry warm water across the Pacific as it begins
Galápagos marine iguanas shrink in length when their algae die back; penguins and sea lions go hungry
In 1972, Peru’s anchoveta fishery, then the world’s largest, collapsed during a strong one plus heavy fishing
NOAA declares one when a key patch of the central Pacific stays at least 0.5 °C above normal for several months
A central-Pacific version is nicknamed Modoki, Japanese for “similar but different”
The TAO array of moored buoys was built after scientists missed the giant 1982–83 event until it was under way
The 2015–16 event helped make 2016 the hottest year measured up to then and helped bleach the Great Barrier Reef
The Pacific jet stream shifts south and strengthens, steering storms toward California and the Gulf Coast

trap.title: El Niño or La Niña?
trap.body: La Niña is the cold phase of the same cycle, with extra-strong trade winds and colder water in the eastern Pacific, so the two share almost every clue: Peru, the trade winds, the Southern Oscillation, and weather effects around the world. Upwelling, the rising cold water that this warm event weakens, is a wrong answer too.
trap.fix: Warm water spreading east, weak trade winds, Christmas, floods in Peru, drought in Australia, and a quiet Atlantic hurricane season mean El Niño. Cold water off South America, extra-strong trade winds, and busier Atlantic hurricane seasons mean La Niña. Saying only “Southern Oscillation” earns a prompt.
trap.line: Real answer line: El Niño (accept El Niño–Southern Oscillation or ENSO; prompt on Southern Oscillation; do not accept “La Niña”)

topics.name: Obsidian
topics.kicker: Natural volcanic glass · Breaks into razor-sharp edges
topics.dates: Named in Pliny the Elder’s _Natural History_, c. 77 CE
topics.briefing: Obsidian is volcanic glass: lava, usually rich in silica, that cooled so quickly its atoms had no time to line up into crystals. It is usually shiny black, and it breaks with smooth, curved surfaces that leave edges sharper than a steel razor. Ancient peoples from Turkey to Mexico chipped it into arrowheads and knives, and some surgeons have even used obsidian scalpels.
topics.answerHtml: Obsidian (prompt on volcanic glass, natural glass, or igneous rock; do not accept “pumice,” “basalt,” or “flint”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In 1960, Irving Friedman and Robert Smith showed how to date artifacts made of this material by measuring the thin water-soaked layer, or hydration rind, that slowly grows on a freshly broken surface. Archaeologists can also trace where a piece came from by its chemical fingerprint.
tossups.r: This material forms when lava cools too quickly for crystals to grow. For 10 points, name this black volcanic glass.

tossups.p: The Elizabethan scholar John Dee owned a polished “magic mirror” made of this material, which was brought to Europe from Mexico after the Spanish conquest and is kept in the British Museum. The Aztec god Tezcatlipoca [“tes-kaht-lee-POH-kah”], whose name means “smoking mirror,” was linked to mirrors of this material.
tossups.r: It breaks with a smooth, curved conchoidal fracture. For 10 points, name this natural volcanic glass that ancient peoples chipped into blades.

tossups.p: Aztec warriors carried the macuahuitl [“mah-KWAH-weetl”], a flat wooden club edged with blades of this material, and the ancient city of Teotihuacan [“tay-oh-tee-wah-KAHN”] grew rich partly by working and trading green examples of it. Much of that green material came from the Sierra de las Navajas, or “Mountains of the Razors,” near Pachuca.
tossups.r: This material is a natural glass that forms when lava cools very quickly. For 10 points, name this rock that ancient peoples chipped into razor-sharp tools.

tossups.p: A water-rich relative of this material, called perlite, puffs up like popcorn when heated and is mixed into potting soil. Rounded, dark lumps of this material called Apache tears are often found inside perlite.
tossups.r: This material forms when silica-rich lava cools too quickly to grow crystals. For 10 points, name this black volcanic glass.

tossups.p: Over millions of years, this material slowly devitrifies, or begins to crystallize, which is why very old examples of it are rare. White, flower-like clusters of tiny crystals give its “snowflake” variety its spots.
tossups.r: This rock has no crystals at first because its lava cooled so fast. For 10 points, name this glassy igneous rock that ancient people made into arrowheads.

tossups.p: Some surgeons have used scalpels made of this material, because a freshly broken edge of it can be just a few nanometers thick, far sharper than a steel blade. Even so, the material is brittle, and its edges chip easily.
tossups.r: Those edges come from its smooth, curved conchoidal fracture. For 10 points, name this black volcanic glass that ancient people chipped into knives and arrowheads.

tossups.p: Pliny the Elder wrote that this material was named for a man called Obsius, who supposedly found it in Ethiopia. Its dark color usually comes from tiny specks of minerals such as magnetite, even though it is rich in pale silica.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this natural glass that forms when lava cools too quickly for crystals to grow.

tossups.p: Native peoples quarried this material at a cliff in Yellowstone National Park, and tools made from that cliff’s stone have been found at Hopewell sites as far away as Ohio. That cliff is named for this material.
tossups.r: This material breaks with a smooth, curved fracture into very sharp edges. For 10 points, name this black volcanic glass.

tossups.p: Oregon’s Newberry Volcano poured out a huge flow of this material about 1,300 years ago, and visitors can hike a trail across its jagged surface. California’s Glass Mountain, near Medicine Lake Volcano, is another huge flow of it.
tossups.r: This material forms from silica-rich lava that cools too quickly to grow crystals. For 10 points, name this glassy, usually black igneous rock.

tossups.p: Polished pieces of this material found at Çatalhöyük [“chah-TAHL-hoo-yook”], a Stone Age town in Turkey, are among the oldest known mirrors, made about 8,000 years ago. Traders carried this material across the ancient Near East from volcanoes in central Turkey.
tossups.r: It breaks with a curved, shell-like fracture. For 10 points, name this natural volcanic glass.

tossups.p: Stone Age sailors crossed the Aegean Sea to collect this material on the Greek island of Melos, and more of it came from Lipari [“LEE-pah-ree”], a volcanic island north of Sicily. Its chemistry lets archaeologists tell which island each piece came from.
tossups.r: Toolmakers chipped this material into sharp blades and arrowheads. For 10 points, name this glassy volcanic rock.

tossups.p: Because this material lacks an orderly arrangement of atoms, many geologists call it a mineraloid rather than a mineral. It usually has about the same silica-rich makeup as rhyolite and granite, and it rates about 5 to 5.5 on the Mohs hardness scale.
tossups.r: It breaks with a curved conchoidal fracture into razor-sharp edges. For 10 points, name this black volcanic glass.

tossups.p: Flintknappers shape this material by pressure flaking, pressing small chips off its edge with the tip of a deer antler. Because it has no grain to follow, it breaks in smooth, predictable curves, letting skilled knappers control each flake.
tossups.r: Ancient peoples from Mexico to the Mediterranean made arrowheads and knives from it. For 10 points, name this black volcanic glass.

tossups.p: Streaks of iron-bearing hematite give the “mahogany” variety of this material its reddish-brown color, while tiny aligned bubbles or crystals give its “sheen” varieties a golden or rainbow shimmer. Polished pieces of these varieties are sold as gemstones.
tossups.r: Ordinary examples of this material are shiny and black. For 10 points, name this natural glass formed when lava cools too fast to grow crystals.

tossups.p: Modern surgeons have used blades of this material for very fine cuts, and Aztec warriors edged wooden clubs with it. It breaks with a smooth, curved, shell-like conchoidal fracture. Unlike frothy pumice, it is dense and has almost no gas bubbles.
tossups.r: This material forms when lava cools too fast for crystals to grow. For 10 points, name this black volcanic glass, prized for sharp arrowheads and blades.

clues.t: Natural volcanic glass, usually shiny black
Forms when lava cools so fast that no crystals can grow
Ancient peoples chipped it into razor-sharp arrowheads, knives, and blades
An extrusive igneous rock with a glassy texture
Breaks with a smooth, curved conchoidal (shell-like) fracture
Usually silica-rich, like rhyolite and granite, but colored dark by tiny specks of magnetite
Freshly broken edges can be a few nanometers thick, so some surgeons have used it for scalpels
A mineraloid, not a true mineral, because its atoms are not orderly; hardness about 5 to 5.5
Pumice is a frothy, bubble-filled volcanic glass that floats; this rock is dense and smooth
Aztec warriors edged the wooden macuahuitl with its blades; Teotihuacan traded green examples
Hydration dating (Irving Friedman and Robert Smith, 1960) measures the water-soaked rind that grows on a broken surface
Each source has a chemical fingerprint, so archaeologists can trace ancient trade routes
John Dee’s “magic mirror” in the British Museum is an Aztec mirror made of it
Tezcatlipoca, the Aztec “Smoking Mirror” god, was linked to its mirrors
Green examples came from the Sierra de las Navajas (“Mountains of the Razors”) near Pachuca
A water-rich relative is perlite, which puffs up when heated; rounded lumps inside perlite are Apache tears
It slowly devitrifies (crystallizes), so very old examples are rare; white crystal clusters make the “snowflake” variety
Pliny the Elder said it was named for Obsius, who found it in Ethiopia
Native peoples quarried it at a Yellowstone cliff; tools from there reached Hopewell sites in Ohio
Oregon’s Newberry Volcano erupted a huge flow of it about 1,300 years ago; California’s Glass Mountain is another
Polished pieces from Çatalhöyük, Turkey, about 8,000 years old, are among the oldest known mirrors
Stone Age sailors traded it from the islands of Melos in Greece and Lipari near Sicily
Flintknappers shape it by pressure flaking, pressing off chips with antler tips
“Mahogany” varieties get reddish-brown streaks from hematite; tiny bubbles or crystals give “sheen” varieties a shimmer

trap.title: Obsidian or pumice?
trap.body: Pumice is volcanic glass too, often with the same silica-rich makeup, so clues about glass, silica, and lava cooling too fast for crystals fit both. Pumice is frothy, full of gas bubbles, and light enough to float, while obsidian is dense and smooth and breaks into sharp edges. Flint, a sedimentary rock that also chips into sharp tools, is another wrong answer.
trap.fix: Sharp blades, arrowheads, mirrors, scalpels, and shiny black glass mean obsidian. Floating, frothy, and full of holes means pumice, and tools chipped from nodules found in chalk mean flint. Saying only “volcanic glass” earns a prompt, so be ready to name the rock.
trap.line: Real answer line: Obsidian (prompt on volcanic glass; do not accept “pumice”)

topics.name: Lakes
topics.kicker: Inland bodies of standing water · Studied in the science of limnology
topics.briefing: A lake is a body of standing water surrounded by land, filling a low spot carved by glaciers, cracked open by moving plates, or left in a volcano’s crater. Russia’s Lake Baikal is the deepest and oldest, Lake Superior covers more area than any other freshwater lake, and the salty Caspian Sea is the largest lake of all. Scientists who study lakes are called limnologists.
topics.answerHtml: Lakes (accept lake; accept specific kinds such as oxbow, crater, glacial, or rift lakes; prompt on reservoirs; do not accept “ponds” or the name of a single lake)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: François-Alphonse Forel [“fuh-REL”], who spent decades studying the waters of Geneva near his Swiss hometown, founded limnology, the science of these bodies of water. Forel also explained seiches [“SAYSH-iz”], the rocking standing waves that slosh back and forth across them.
tossups.r: Russia’s Baikal is the deepest of them. For 10 points, name these inland bodies of standing water, such as Superior and Titicaca.

tossups.p: Scientists lower a black-and-white Secchi [“SEK-ee”] disk into one of these bodies of water to measure how clear it is. The shallow edge of one, where rooted plants grow, is its littoral zone, while its deep, dark bottom water is the profundal zone.
tossups.r: Cold air crossing these bodies of water can dump heavy snow on cities downwind, like Buffalo. For 10 points, name these inland bodies of standing water, such as Superior and Victoria.

tossups.p: In summer, many of these bodies of water split into a warm upper layer called the epilimnion [“ep-ih-LIM-nee-on”] and a cold lower hypolimnion [“hy-poh-LIM-nee-on”], separated by a thermocline. In spring and fall, their layers mix in an event called turnover.
tossups.r: Because water is densest at about 4 °C, ice forms on their surfaces first. For 10 points, name these bodies of standing water, such as Superior and Baikal.

tossups.p: In the 1960s, one of these bodies of water became so choked with algae, fed by phosphates from detergents and fertilizer, that newspapers declared it “dead,” a famous case of eutrophication. Rotting algae used up the oxygen in its deep water, leaving zones where fish could not live.
tossups.r: That body of water, Erie, is one of five connected giants in North America, along with Superior and Michigan. For 10 points, name these inland bodies of standing water.

tossups.p: In 1986, a huge cloud of carbon dioxide burst out of Cameroon’s Nyos, one of these bodies of water, in a rare event called a limnic eruption, killing about 1,700 people nearby. Pipes were later installed to release the gas safely from its depths.
tossups.r: Most of these bodies of water hold fresh water. For 10 points, name these inland bodies of standing water, such as Baikal and Superior.

tossups.p: In 2012, Russian drillers reached Vostok, the largest of many bodies of water hidden beneath Antarctica’s ice sheet, after boring through nearly 4 kilometers of ice. Scientists hope its dark, cold water may hold microbes sealed off for a very long time.
tossups.r: Russia also has Baikal, the deepest of these bodies of water. For 10 points, name these inland bodies of standing water.

tossups.p: The nerpa, one of the few seals that live only in fresh water, swims in one of these bodies of water in Siberia, which holds about a fifth of the world’s unfrozen surface fresh water. It sits in a rift valley where the crust is slowly pulling apart.
tossups.r: That body of water, Baikal, is the oldest and deepest of its kind. For 10 points, name these inland bodies of standing water, which also include Superior.

tossups.p: About 7,700 years ago, Mount Mazama in Oregon erupted and collapsed into a caldera that slowly filled with rain and snowmelt, forming the deepest of these bodies of water in the United States. No rivers flow into or out of it.
tossups.r: That one is named for the crater-like bowl it fills. For 10 points, name these bodies of standing water, which also include oxbow and glacial types.

tossups.p: During the last ice age, Bonneville, a huge body of water covering much of western Utah, burst through Red Rock Pass in Idaho and sent a giant flood roaring down the Snake River. Its salty leftovers still lie in northern Utah.
tossups.r: Ones with no outlet, like the Dead Sea, turn salty as their water evaporates. For 10 points, name these inland bodies of standing water.

tossups.p: As North America’s great ice sheets melted, they left behind Agassiz, a gigantic body of meltwater named for Louis Agassiz. Glacial bodies of water like it collected thin yearly layers of sediment called varves, which scientists count like tree rings.
tossups.r: Ice-age glaciers also helped carve out the basins of Superior and Michigan. For 10 points, name these bodies of standing water, which include kettle and oxbow types.

tossups.p: The Uros people live on floating islands made of totora [“toh-TOR-uh”] reeds in one of these bodies of water, which sits about 3,800 meters above sea level on the border of Peru and Bolivia. In Inca legend, the founders of their empire rose from its waters.
tossups.r: That body of water, Titicaca, is often called the highest navigable one in the world. For 10 points, name these inland bodies of standing water, the deepest of which is Baikal.

tossups.p: In 1858, John Hanning Speke reached the largest of these bodies of water in Africa and named it for his queen, correctly guessing that it was the main source of the White Nile. His former traveling partner, the explorer Richard Burton, refused to accept that claim.
tossups.r: Tanganyika and Malawi are long, deep examples of these bodies of water in Africa’s Great Rift Valley. For 10 points, name these inland bodies of standing water.

tossups.p: Gordon Lightfoot wrote a hit song about the freighter _Edmund Fitzgerald_, which sank with all 29 of its crew during a November storm in 1975 while carrying iron ore across one of these bodies of water. The ship’s bell was later raised from the wreck and placed in a museum as a memorial.
tossups.r: That body of water, Superior, has the largest surface area of any freshwater one. For 10 points, name these inland bodies of standing water, whose deepest example is Russia’s Baikal.

tossups.p: Soviet irrigation projects diverted the Amu Darya and Syr Darya rivers to grow cotton, causing the Aral Sea, once one of the largest of these bodies of water, to shrink to a small fraction of its former size.
tossups.r: The Caspian Sea, bordered by five countries including Russia and Iran, is the largest of these bodies of water. For 10 points, name these inland bodies of standing water.

tossups.p: These bodies of water can form when a winding river cuts off one of its loops, when a glacier gouges out a basin, or when rain fills a volcano’s crater. Ponds are usually smaller and shallow enough for sunlight to reach the bottom everywhere.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these inland bodies of standing water, such as Superior, Victoria, and Baikal.

clues.t: Inland bodies of standing water surrounded by land
Russia’s Baikal, in Siberia, is the deepest and oldest, and holds the most fresh water
Superior is the largest freshwater one by surface area
The salty Caspian Sea is the largest of all by area
Kinds include oxbow, crater, glacial, and rift types
Oxbow types form when a winding river cuts off one of its loops, or meanders
The deepest one in the U.S. fills the caldera of Oregon’s Mount Mazama, which collapsed about 7,700 years ago; no rivers flow in or out
Ice-age glaciers helped carve the basins of Superior, Michigan, Huron, Erie, and Ontario
Eutrophication: nutrient runoff feeds algae that use up the oxygen, as in Erie in the 1960s
Ones with no outlet, like the Dead Sea, turn salty as their water evaporates
In summer, a warm epilimnion sits over a cold hypolimnion, split by a thermocline; spring and fall turnover mixes them
Water is densest at about 4 °C, so ice forms on top and life survives below
Titicaca, on the Peru–Bolivia border at about 3,800 m, has floating reed islands built by the Uros people
Victoria, Africa’s largest, is the main source of the White Nile; John Hanning Speke named it in 1858
Cold air crossing their open water can dump heavy snow on cities downwind, like Buffalo
Ponds are usually smaller and shallow enough for sunlight to reach the bottom everywhere
François-Alphonse Forel founded limnology, their science, by studying the waters of Geneva
Seiches are rocking standing waves that slosh back and forth across them
A Secchi disk measures their clarity; zones run from the shallow littoral to the dark, deep profundal
In 1986, Cameroon’s Nyos released a cloud of carbon dioxide in a limnic eruption that killed about 1,700 people
Vostok is the largest one hidden under Antarctica’s ice; Russian drillers reached it in 2012
Baikal’s nerpa is one of the few seals that live only in fresh water; Baikal holds about a fifth of the world’s unfrozen surface fresh water
Ice-age Bonneville covered much of western Utah and burst through Red Rock Pass in Idaho in a giant flood
Melting ice sheets left the giant Agassiz; glacial ones collect yearly layers of sediment called varves
The freighter _Edmund Fitzgerald_ sank on Superior with all 29 crew in 1975, inspiring a Gordon Lightfoot song
Soviet irrigation from the Amu Darya and Syr Darya rivers made the Aral Sea shrink
Inca legend says the founders of their empire rose from Titicaca’s waters
The explorer Richard Burton refused to accept Speke’s claim that Victoria was the source of the Nile

trap.title: Category, not one example
trap.body: Lake tossups love to name famous examples, like Baikal, Superior, Titicaca, and the Caspian Sea, so players blurt out one name, which is wrong when the question wants the whole category. Neighboring answers trip players up too: ponds are smaller and shallow enough for sunlight to reach the bottom, and rivers flow while lakes stand still.
trap.fix: Listen for “these bodies of water” or “these features” and answer lakes. Naming a kind, like oxbow lakes or crater lakes, is fine. If the tossup says “this lake” and its clues all point to one place, it wants that specific lake instead.
trap.line: Real answer line: Lakes (accept lake or specific kinds such as oxbow lakes; do not accept the name of one specific lake)

topics.name: Sand
topics.kicker: Loose grains between silt and gravel in size · Mostly bits of quartz
topics.briefing: Sand is made of loose grains of rock and mineral bigger than silt but smaller than gravel, from 1/16 of a millimeter to 2 millimeters across. Most beach and desert sand is quartz, tough enough to survive after other minerals wear away, but Hawaii has black sand made of volcanic glass and Bermuda has pink sand made of tiny shells. Melt quartz sand with a few other ingredients and you get glass.
topics.answerHtml: Sand (accept sands or specific kinds such as beach sand; prompt on sediment; do not accept “quartz,” “silt,” “gravel,” or “sandstone”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Archimedes invented a way to write enormous numbers in a work estimating how many grains of this material it would take to fill the entire universe. He arrived at a figure of about 10 to the 63rd power grains.
tossups.r: This material’s grains are coarser than silt but finer than gravel. For 10 points, name this loose material that covers beaches and deserts.

tossups.p: In 1922, Chester Wentworth set the size range of this material’s grains at 1/16 of a millimeter to 2 millimeters across, and William Krumbein later turned that scale into simple “phi” numbers. Wentworth built on an earlier scale by Johan August Udden.
tossups.r: Grains finer than this material are silt, and coarser ones are gravel. For 10 points, name this loose material that covers beaches and fills hourglasses.

tossups.p: Some dunes, like California’s Kelso Dunes and China’s Mingsha Shan, a ridge of dunes named for its singing, boom or hum loudly when grains of this material avalanche down their steep slopes. The effect needs dry, well-rounded, evenly sized grains.
tossups.r: Most of this material is made of quartz. For 10 points, name this granular material that wind piles into desert dunes.

tossups.p: When lightning strikes this material, the heat can fuse it into hollow, branching tubes called fulgurites, and the 1945 Trinity atomic test in New Mexico fused it into a greenish crust called trinitite.
tossups.r: Glassmakers melt this material, mostly silica, with soda ash and lime. For 10 points, name this granular material found on beaches and in deserts.

tossups.p: Ralph Bagnold’s 1941 book on desert dunes explained saltation, the way wind lifts grains of this material and drops them in short, bouncing hops. Bagnold had explored the deserts of Egypt and Libya by car in the 1920s and 1930s.
tossups.r: Wind piles this material into crescent-shaped dunes called barchans. For 10 points, name this loose material whose grains are between 1/16 and 2 millimeters across.

tossups.p: Wind-blown grains of this material make poor concrete, because the wind has rounded and polished them so smooth that they do not lock together well. Some countries covered in dunes even import this material from overseas for construction.
tossups.r: Builders mix this material with gravel, water, and cement to make concrete. For 10 points, name this granular material found on beaches.

tossups.p: Parrotfish grind up coral as they feed, and the crushed coral they leave behind makes up much of the white form of this material on tropical islands. Bermuda’s pink shores get their color from the shells of tiny red foraminifera [“fuh-ram-uh-NIF-er-uh”].
tossups.r: On most other beaches, this material is mostly quartz. For 10 points, name this loose, grainy material that also forms desert dunes.

tossups.p: The shore at Hawaii’s Papakōlea [“pah-pah-koh-LAY-ah”] is green because its grains are olivine crystals, while black shores elsewhere in Hawaii formed when hot lava shattered into tiny bits of glass as it hit the sea.
tossups.r: This material’s grains are coarser than silt but finer than gravel. For 10 points, name this granular material that covers beaches and fills hourglasses.

tossups.p: Arabia’s Rub’ al Khali, or Empty Quarter, is the largest continuous sea of this material on Earth, a kind of desert called an erg. Most of the Sahara, by contrast, is bare rock and gravel.
tossups.r: Wind piles this material into dunes. For 10 points, name this loose material made mostly of quartz grains.

tossups.p: Dunes of this material in Namibia’s Namib Desert are among the tallest in the world, and a thin coating of iron oxide on each grain gives them their red-orange color. The famous red dunes around Sossusvlei, a usually dry clay pan, draw many visitors.
tossups.r: Glass is made by melting this material. For 10 points, name this granular material found on beaches and in deserts.

tossups.p: William Blake’s poem “Auguries of Innocence” opens by asking readers to see a world in a single grain of this material and a heaven in a wild flower. Its next lines tell readers to hold infinity in the palm of their hand.
tossups.r: Hourglasses measure time with falling grains of this material. For 10 points, name this loose, granular material that covers beaches.

tossups.p: When granite weathers, its feldspar breaks down into clay, but its toughest mineral grains survive, wash downstream, and pile up as this material. Grains carried far by rivers or wind become well rounded and evenly sized, or “well sorted.”
tossups.r: Cemented grains of this material form a common sedimentary rock. For 10 points, name this material whose grains are between silt and gravel in size.

tossups.p: The Navajo formation of Utah and Arizona preserves giant ancient dunes made of this material, whose slanting layers, called cross-beds, show which way the wind blew. The rose-red city of Petra in Jordan was carved into cliffs of rock made from it.
tossups.r: Wind and waves pile this material into dunes and beaches. For 10 points, name this loose, grainy material made mostly of quartz.

tossups.p: Longshore drift carries this material along a coastline in a zigzag path, building long spits and barrier islands, and engineers build walls called groins to trap it. In winter, big storm waves often pull it offshore.
tossups.r: This material covers most beaches and many deserts. For 10 points, name this loose material whose grains are coarser than silt but finer than gravel.

tossups.p: Its grains are coarser than silt but finer than gravel, and builders mix it with gravel and cement to make concrete. Over time, its grains can be cemented together into a common sedimentary rock.
tossups.r: Wind piles it into dunes, and glassmakers melt it down. For 10 points, name this granular material, mostly made of quartz, that covers beaches.

clues.t: Loose, grainy material covering beaches and parts of deserts
Glass is made by melting it (mostly silica) with soda ash and lime
Hourglasses measure time with its falling grains
Most of it is grains of quartz, the tough mineral that survives weathering
Wentworth scale (1922): grains 1/16 mm to 2 mm across, coarser than silt and finer than gravel
Mixed with gravel, cement, and water to make concrete
Its grains cemented together make a sedimentary rock, as in Utah’s Navajo formation and Petra’s carved cliffs
Hawaii has black kinds made of volcanic glass that shattered when lava hit the sea
Wind piles it into dunes, such as crescent-shaped barchans
Longshore drift carries it along coasts to build spits and barrier islands; groins trap it
When granite weathers, feldspar becomes clay, but the toughest grains survive as this material
Grains carried far by wind or water become well rounded and well sorted
Archimedes estimated that about 10 to the 63rd power of its grains would fill the universe
Wentworth built on Johan August Udden’s scale; William Krumbein turned grain sizes into “phi” numbers
“Singing” or booming dunes, like California’s Kelso Dunes and China’s Mingsha Shan, hum when grains avalanche
Lightning fuses it into hollow, branching tubes called fulgurites
The 1945 Trinity atomic test fused it into a greenish crust called trinitite
Ralph Bagnold’s 1941 book explained saltation, the short hops of wind-blown grains; he had explored Egypt’s and Libya’s deserts by car
Wind-polished desert grains are too smooth and round to make good concrete
Parrotfish grind coral into white grains; Bermuda’s pink beaches come from red foraminifera shells
Hawaii’s Papakōlea Beach is green from olivine crystals
Arabia’s Rub’ al Khali (Empty Quarter) is the largest erg, or sea of it; most of the Sahara is rock and gravel instead
Namibia’s Namib dunes, among the world’s tallest, are colored red-orange by iron oxide coatings
William Blake’s “Auguries of Innocence” asks readers to see a world in one of its grains
In the Bahamas, tiny round ooids of aragonite grow layer by layer to form a white kind

trap.title: Sand, not quartz
trap.body: Sand tossups describe what its grains are made of, especially quartz, so players buzz with “quartz,” which names the mineral, not the loose material. Others answer with a neighboring grain size: silt is finer, and gravel is coarser. Sandstone, the rock made of cemented grains, and dunes, the hills that wind builds from it, are different answers too.
trap.fix: Listen for “this material” plus a grain size of 1/16 to 2 millimeters, beaches, dunes, hourglasses, or glassmaking, and answer sand. Six-sided crystals, piezoelectricity, and a Mohs hardness of 7 mean quartz. Saying only “sediment” earns a prompt.
trap.line: Real answer line: Sand (prompt on sediment; do not accept “quartz,” “silt,” or “sandstone”)
